strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: avoiding uninformative tasks during reinforcement finetuning without adding online rollouts.
BOTS is simple and computationally lightweight at training time. Combining discounted direct observations with reference-model predictions is intuitive and potentially useful.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering math, code, and logic with 1.5B and 7B models. The paper also includes ablations over the evidence-mixing and forgetting coefficients, posterior sampling, wall-clock overhead, estimator quality, and selected-task dynamics.
The visualizations provide evidence that BOTS increases the fraction of nontrivial training tasks, and some experiments show faster attainment of the random baseline's peak performance.
The manuscript is generally organized clearly and provides substantial implementation detail for the underlying GRPO training.
weaknesses: There are serious errors and contradictions in the core method description. Section 3.4 defines utility as |p-p*| and says to select the highest utility, which selects tasks farthest from the target difficulty, contradicting the intended closest-to-target selection. The text also alternately claims that smaller and larger lambda cause faster forgetting; only the latter follows from the stated update.

Proposition 2 is false as stated. Its proof establishes only uniform lower and upper bounds, not that the liminf and limsup equal those bounds for an arbitrary task-selection sequence. For example, periodic selection generally produces limits or cycles strictly inside the claimed extrema. Thus, an advertised theoretical characterization is invalid.

The Bayesian interpretation is limited. The task success probability changes whenever the policy is updated, but no probabilistic transition model connects these changing parameters. The update is better viewed as a heuristic discounted estimator, and standard Thompson-sampling guarantees do not directly apply to moving arms, target-distance selection, and model-generated pseudo-observations.

The experimental comparison lacks strong actual online-selection baselines. BOTS-MoPPS is a parameter setting within the proposed implementation, while BOTS-DOTS is explicitly only a proxy that replaces DOTS's estimator and omits trajectory replay. Consequently, these experiments mainly compare BOTS variants rather than establish superiority over the cited methods.

Statistical reliability is inadequate. No results across independent training seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are reported. This is particularly problematic for AIME24 and for the proposed TTB and best-so-far metrics, which are sensitive to noisy single-run peaks. The plotted bands are not explained.

The presentation emphasizes counts of first- and second-place finishes across many correlated relative metrics. Absolute final-performance gains are often small or absent: aggregate BSF at full budget is approximately 1.00-1.05, and competing variants frequently match or outperform full BOTS. This does not convincingly support claims of consistent superiority.

The claimed negligible cost excludes the potentially substantial offline expense of evaluating two reference models on every task. This cost is merely assumed to be already available, weakening the general efficiency claim. There is also no ablation over reference-model choice despite the method's acknowledged dependence on it.

Reproducibility has important gaps and inconsistencies: the Beta prior and momentum coefficient are not specified, the code-release URL is blank, and different sections identify the second reference model as Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-8B, or Qwen3-32B. These ambiguities materially affect the central interpolator.

Overall, the practical idea is promising, but the incorrect theory, internally inconsistent algorithm specification, weak baseline controls, and lack of replicated evidence prevent the paper from meeting a top-tier acceptance standard.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: avoiding trivial or currently unsolvable tasks during reinforcement finetuning.
BOTS combines discounted Beta updates, explicit rollout outcomes, interpolated pseudo-observations, and posterior sampling into a computationally simple framework.

The evaluation spans three domains and two model sizes, with ablations for the evidence-mixing and forgetting coefficients, an interpolator analysis, task-selection visualizations, and an online runtime breakdown.

weaknesses: The central selection rule is internally inconsistent. Section 3.4 defines utility as |p-p*| and says to select the highest-utility tasks, which selects probabilities farthest from p*=0.5—the opposite of the stated goal and of the later description of selecting the closest tasks. This makes the formal algorithm incorrect or, at minimum, unreproducible.

Proposition 2 is false as stated. The proof establishes uniform lower and upper bounds, but those bounds do not imply that every selection trajectory has the claimed limiting infimum and supremum. A task that is always selected, for example, converges only to the upper endpoint. The paper also repeatedly reverses the effect of lambda: under the given recurrence, larger lambda causes faster forgetting and a smaller effective sample size, contrary to several theoretical explanations.

The empirical comparison is inadequate for the main claims. DOTS is replaced by a proxy using the authors' own interpolator, MoPPS is represented by a parameter setting, and oversampling/filtering approaches motivating the claimed efficiency advantage are not compared directly on end-to-end wall-clock performance.

No number of independent runs, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests is reported. Many differences are small or inconsistent, particularly for the 7B model, while BOTS-DOTS or other variants frequently match or outperform full BOTS. The paper nevertheless uses language such as "significantly" and "consistently" without statistical support.

The custom TTB and BSF ratios are sensitive to noise in a single random-baseline trajectory and to small denominators. Reporting many correlated fractions and counting first- and second-place finishes does not substitute for absolute scores with uncertainty. Posterior sampling itself produces essentially no downstream improvement in the reported ablation.

The negligible-overhead claim excludes the potentially substantial offline cost of obtaining per-task success rates from two large reference models. Assuming these exact metadata already exist may be practical for GURU, but does not establish end-to-end efficiency for a new dataset.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the advertised code-release footnote contains no link; important quantities such as the Beta prior and momentum coefficient are not clearly specified; and the reference-model descriptions conflict across the paper (Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-32B).

The novelty is modest: the main components are standard discounted conjugate updates, linear interpolation, and Thompson sampling. Given the formal errors, weak baseline coverage, and lack of statistically reliable evidence, the submission is not competitive at the stated acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: avoiding uninformative tasks during reinforcement fine-tuning without adding online rollouts. Combining historical explicit feedback with cross-task implicit estimates is intuitive and potentially useful.

BOTS is presented as a modular framework: the Beta-Bernoulli posterior, evidence mixing, forgetting, and posterior sampling form a coherent high-level design, while the implicit estimator can in principle be replaced.

The empirical study is broad in domain and scale, covering math, code, and logic with both 1.5B and 7B models. Ablations over the evidence weight, forgetting factor, and posterior sampling help expose the behavior of individual components.

The selected-task analyses provide useful evidence that BOTS reduces sampling of zero-reward and fully mastered tasks. The reported online selection overhead is also very small once reference-model statistics are available.
The paper is generally well organized and candidly discusses limitations of linear interpolation, reference-model choice, and selection-induced bias.
weaknesses: Section 3.4 contains a central sign/direction error: it defines utility as |p-p*| and selects tasks with the highest utility, which selects tasks farthest from the target difficulty, despite repeatedly claiming to select the closest tasks. The appendix instead describes closest-rate selection. This makes the formal algorithm inconsistent with both its motivation and apparent implementation.

Proposition 2 is false as stated. Its proof establishes uniform lower and upper bounds, but these do not imply that an arbitrary task-selection sequence has liminf and limsup equal to those bounds. Equality is shown only for special never-selected and always-selected sequences. Several interpretations based on this proposition are therefore unsupported.

The discussion of lambda is internally contradictory. From the update, smaller lambda means slower forgetting and larger effective sample size, whereas Section 3.4 and Appendix E.1 claim that smaller lambda accelerates forgetting. Section 4.3 gives the opposite, apparently correct interpretation.

Experimental uncertainty is not reported: there are no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Given the noisy RL setting and often small final BSF differences—frequently only a few percent—it is difficult to know whether the downstream gains are reliable.

The comparison does not faithfully implement several strongest related methods. BOTS-DOTS is explicitly only a proxy using the authors' interpolator, and BOTS-MoPPS is an in-framework configuration; oversampling-based online selectors are not included. Consequently, the claim of outperforming competitive existing approaches is stronger than the evidence.

The results are less consistent than the narrative suggests: BOTS is not the best method on numerous domain/model/metric combinations, occasionally underperforms random sampling, and implicit-only or explicit-only variants can match or exceed it. This points to substantial domain dependence and weakens the claim that evidence fusion is uniformly preferable.

The claimed negligible cost excludes the potentially substantial offline evaluation of every task with two large reference models. The paper assumes these statistics already exist, so the end-to-end efficiency claim needs a separate accounting or an amortization analysis.

Reproducibility details are inconsistent or incomplete: different sections name Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-32B, and Qwen3-8B as reference or tie-breaking models; the first-page code-release footnote has no visible URL; and the dependence on precomputed per-task success rates is not specified sufficiently. Overall, the idea and experimental breadth are promising, but the mathematical errors and lack of statistically rigorous, faithful baseline comparisons place the submission slightly below the acceptance threshold.
